overview:
Egypt sits in the northeastern corner of Africa, with its Sinai Peninsula reaching into Asia, so it is a bridge between two continents. The country is about one and a half times the size of Texas, but almost all of it is desert. Life clings to the Nile River, which runs the whole length of the country, and to its fan-shaped delta on the Mediterranean; around 95 percent of Egyptians live on about 5 percent of the land. The capital, Cairo, is a roaring metropolis of more than 20 million people, with the pyramids of Giza standing at its western edge.

Egypt has around 110 million people, the most of any Arab country. Arabic is the official language, and most Egyptians are Sunni Muslim, with a large Coptic Christian community whose church dates back nearly 2,000 years. Egypt is a republic with a president and a powerful military. Farming, tourism, the Suez Canal, and natural gas support the economy. Egyptians are proud of one of the oldest civilizations on Earth and of their modern role at the center of Arab music, film, and culture.
landAndNature: The Nile, the longest river in Africa, flows north through a green ribbon of fields just a few kilometers wide before spreading into the delta. West of it lies the Western Desert, part of the Sahara, with oases like Siwa, the strange chalk formations of the White Desert, and the Qattara Depression, 133 meters below sea level. East of the Nile the rocky Eastern Desert rises to hills along the Red Sea, whose coral reefs are among the most colorful in the world. The Sinai Peninsula has rugged red mountains; Mount Catherine, at 2,629 meters, is Egypt's highest point. Rain is rare almost everywhere. Camels, fennec foxes, and Egyptian cobras live in the deserts, and Lake Nasser behind the Aswan High Dam has Nile crocodiles.
peopleAndCulture: Egyptians speak a lively dialect of Arabic understood across the Arab world thanks to Cairo's movies and pop songs. Family gatherings feature koshari, a street dish of rice, lentils, pasta, and crispy onions, ful medames, slow-cooked beans eaten at breakfast, and stuffed pigeon for celebrations. During Ramadan, streets glow with colorful lanterns called fanous, and families break their fast at sunset feasts. Soccer is a national obsession; the Pharaohs have won the Africa Cup of Nations a record seven times. Egypt also dominates world squash. Singer Umm Kulthum, whose concerts once stopped traffic, remains beloved, and Naguib Mahfouz won the Nobel Prize in Literature. Coptic Christians celebrate Christmas on January 7.
history: About 5,000 years ago King Narmer united Upper and Lower Egypt, beginning a civilization of pharaohs that lasted nearly 3,000 years. Its people built the pyramids, carved hieroglyphs, mummified their dead, and invented papyrus paper and a 365-day calendar. Alexander the Great conquered Egypt in 332 BC, and after Cleopatra's death in 30 BC it became a Roman province. Arab armies brought Islam and the Arabic language in 641. The Ottoman Empire ruled from 1517, and Britain occupied the country from 1882. Egypt became a kingdom in 1922 and a republic in 1953 after officers led by Gamal Abdel Nasser overthrew the king. Nasser took control of the Suez Canal in 1956. A popular uprising in 2011 toppled longtime president Hosni Mubarak, and the military returned to power in 2013.
funFacts: The Great Pyramid of Giza was the tallest structure made by humans for about 3,800 years.
Ancient Egyptians loved cats so much that they mummified them, and killing one could be punished by death.
Egypt has more than 100 pyramids, not just the three famous ones at Giza.
The Suez Canal, opened in 1869, saves ships about 7,000 kilometers compared with sailing around Africa.
The Rosetta Stone, found in Egypt in 1799, carried the same text in three scripts and unlocked the reading of hieroglyphs.
